forces: Two violins, two violas and two cellos
performers: Hollywood String Quartet (Felix Slatkin and Paul Shure, violins; Paul Robyn, viola; Eleanor Aller, cello); Alvin Dinkin, viola; Kurt Reher, cello
question: How can six strings change the emotional meaning of a phrase without changing the ensemble?
intro: Six individual strings follow the changing emotional world of Richard Dehmel’s poem: a woman tells her companion that she is carrying another man’s child. This is the first side of the original sextet recording, not a separate movement. The LP break falls between bars 228 and 229, before the D-major answer heard on side 2.

cues.title: Lower strings begin the walk
cues.text: The sextet begins with violas and cellos, before the violins join. A descending figure moves over repeated low notes; the writing separates a moving line from the steadier tread beneath it.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score, bars 1–9, ASC copy E1 pp. 2–3, inspected directly. The analysis begins quietly in D minor. The cue identifies opening scoring, not a separated audio stem.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Six voices, not a section
cues.text: There are two violins, two violas and two cellos. Try following a lower moving line instead of treating all the strings beneath the top melody as one undifferentiated accompaniment.
cues.evidence: Original score and Capitol sleeve establish six independent players. No voice entrance is asserted at 0:38.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The poem behind the music
cues.text: Dehmel’s “Transfigured Night” appeared in his 1896 collection Weib und Welt. Two people walk beneath the moon; the woman confesses her pregnancy, and the man later accepts the child. The instruments suggest their emotional changes without spoken or sung words.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Center work essay by Therese Muxeneder reproduces the poem and explains its five sections: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4

cues.title: The first large expansion
cues.text: The initially restrained sound opens into a much stronger wave, then draws back. Listen for how a connected phrase can gain urgency through intensity and register rather than through the arrival of a different instrumental family.
cues.evidence: The report rises between 2:00 and 2:15, then falls sharply around 2:20. Register and connected phrasing are score-informed general features; the timed claim is the relative-level expansion.

cues.title: Follow the leaning notes
cues.text: Many phrases lean on a note that presses against the accompanying harmony before moving on. Listen for those delayed resolutions: chromatic motion can keep a tonal phrase unsettled without abandoning its destination.
cues.evidence: The original sextet score and Schoenberg’s 1950 analysis show chromatic, tonal thematic writing. This is a listening strategy, not an asserted chord identification at 2:32.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: An autumn in Payerbach
cues.text: Schoenberg composed the work in 1899, around a stay in Payerbach with Alexander Zemlinsky and Mathilde Zemlinsky. The surviving score is dated 1 December: the piece belongs to his early tonal music, not to his later twelve-note method.
cues.evidence: The Arnold Schönberg Center work essay and work catalogue date composition to September–1 December 1899 and identify the Payerbach stay: https://schoenberg.at/en/schoenberg/kompositionen/transfigured-night-op-4; https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=420&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: Another crest has receded
cues.text: A second strong expansion has fallen back into a quieter paragraph. Compare the repeated pattern of gathering and release with a single, uninterrupted crescendo: the confession advances through changing states rather than a straight rise in volume.
cues.evidence: The report is strong through 3:05–3:20 and drops substantially at 3:30. A structural-change peak at 4:02 follows the withdrawal.

cues.title: An inward contrasting passage
cues.text: The quieter material gives the sextet a different balance after the preceding outbursts. Listen for shorter exchanges within the continuing string sound; a new episode need not announce itself with a new tempo or a complete silence.
cues.evidence: The report changes strongly at 4:02 and stays at a lower level through the following span, with another change at 4:46. The section label describes the recording’s contrasting paragraph, not a precisely aligned poetic stanza.

cues.title: A chamber premiere in Vienna
cues.text: The first performance took place in Vienna’s small Musikverein hall on 18 March 1902. The Rosé Quartet was joined by Franz Jelinek on viola and Franz Schmidt on cello — the same six-part scoring heard here, not the later string-orchestra arrangement.
cues.evidence: Arnold Schönberg Center work catalogue, premiere entry and programme reference 4892: https://archive2.schoenberg.at/compositions/werke_einzelansicht.php?werke_id=420&herkunft=allewerke

cues.title: The texture regains force
cues.text: The quieter episode has opened into another forceful stretch. Keep the separate upper and lower lines in mind as the sound thickens: six independent parts can create a much larger apparent weight than their number suggests.
cues.evidence: The report rises sharply near 5:10 and reaches strong windows at 5:25–5:35. The source and score establish six independent strings; no particular doubling is timed here.

cues.title: A crest before the contrast
cues.text: A further expansion approaches one of this side’s strongest points. Listen beyond the crest for the change in harmonic colour and the lower level that follow it.
cues.evidence: The report’s 6:30–6:40 windows are among the loudest and brightest, then fall around 6:55. The following E-major episode is established from the score, not merely from automated key estimates.

cues.title: A contrasting major region
cues.text: An E-major episode offers a gentler contrast within the woman’s account. Schoenberg’s own explanation connects this theme with her longing for fulfilment; it is not yet the D-major answer that begins the second LP side.
cues.evidence: The composer’s analysis, reproduced by the ASC, identifies the fourth theme in E major. Original score pp. 12–13 shows the move into that region. Report changes at 6:52 and 7:08 accompany the quieter major-coloured span.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Calm still contains motion
cues.text: Even in the gentler episode, the inner parts do not simply hold a chord. Follow a small moving figure beneath the longer melody and notice how it keeps the phrase active while the overall sound remains quieter.
cues.evidence: Original sextet score p. 13, Etwas ruhiger, combines longer upper phrases with moving viola and cello figures. The report’s 7:00–7:55 span is generally quieter than the preceding crest; placement is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The composer wrote the notes
cues.text: Schoenberg supplied the programme notes for this Capitol LP. The sleeve also says that the recording was prepared under his personal supervision; that is the label’s documented account, not evidence that he attended every moment of the sessions.
cues.evidence: Original Capitol L-8118 sleeve and Arnold Schönberg Audio Archive record entry: https://archive.schoenberg.at/av/tontraeger.php?id_tontraeger=870&action=view. The sleeve’s supervision claim is preserved with its attribution.

cues.title: A retreat inside the paragraph
cues.text: The later middle span repeatedly lowers its intensity before growing again. Listen through the retreat rather than treating the quieter passage as a break in the argument.
cues.evidence: The report drops around 8:35 and then rebuilds through the following windows. This describes a local contour within the section, not an exact thematic return.

cues.title: The bass keeps moving
cues.text: Try listening from the bottom upward. A changing bass can alter the meaning of a sustained upper note, while a repeated bass can hold the phrase in place beneath more restless inner voices.
cues.evidence: The original sextet score repeatedly distinguishes the second cello’s bass from the first cello and viola counterlines. This is a general listening invitation without a timestamped bass-note claim.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Several waves, one ensemble
cues.text: The sextet gathers into another broad expansion. The change is made by the same six players: dynamics, spacing and the number of simultaneously active lines can alter the apparent size of the sound.
cues.evidence: The report builds towards strong windows at 10:20 and 10:35. Instrument count comes from the original scoring and sleeve; automatic onset counts are not used because the transfer has surface scratches.

cues.title: The sound drops away
cues.text: After that expansion the recording withdraws again, leaving a more exposed passage. Listen for how much of the earlier pressure survives in quieter phrases rather than equating reduced volume with a settled conclusion.
cues.evidence: A report boundary at 10:56 accompanies a drop through 11:05–11:15. The cue identifies relative level, not a new key or an exact instrumental entry.

cues.title: Remember the opening figure
cues.text: Keep the descending figure from the opening in memory as the later phrases change shape. Schoenberg’s method repeatedly transforms related ideas; recognition need not depend on a literal, note-for-note repeat.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s analysis relates later passages to earlier themes and identifies a return to the opening’s atmosphere. No exact recurrence is claimed at 11:24.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Agitation returns in waves
cues.text: This later stretch alternates restraint with renewed force. The music has not yet reached the man’s answer: the first side still belongs to the unsettled world that precedes the D-major change.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 11:38 and 11:56 precede a quiet stretch and a steep rise around 12:25. The side boundary before bar 229 is established separately from the inspected score and tonal endpoints.

cues.title: A last forceful expansion
cues.text: The first side gathers into a final substantial wave before its long withdrawal. Compare its connected intensity with the increasingly separated gestures that follow.
cues.evidence: The report rises sharply at 12:25 and remains relatively strong through 13:00, followed by a major change at 13:06. No single climax note is singled out.

cues.title: Strong and quiet replies
cues.text: Shorter spans now alternate between force and restraint. Listen for the gaps in weight between gestures: the phrase is loosening its hold before the suspended ending of the side.
cues.evidence: Five-second windows alternate markedly around 13:15–13:35, with quieter points around 13:15, 13:25 and 13:35. The score’s late first-half gestures support the passage description.

cues.title: E♭ minor gives way to B♭
cues.text: The first half settles into E♭ minor and finally leaves B♭ suspended in the bass. Schoenberg uses that remaining note as the link to the contrasting D-major music on the next side.
cues.evidence: Schoenberg’s own analysis explicitly describes E♭ minor and the remaining B♭. Original sextet score pp. 24–25, bars 204–228, inspected; the report’s quiet 14:10–14:40 tail is dominated by the corresponding pitch classes. This is a passage-level endpoint, not a precisely timed chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A side break, not an ending
cues.text: The LP stops after bar 228. Continue directly with side 2 for the D-major answer at bar 229: the physical division of the record interrupts one continuous composition.
cues.evidence: ASC original score pp. 25–26: the B♭ at the end of bar 228 is followed by the D-major Sehr breit und langsam at bar 229. The analysed first-side tail and second-side D-major opening match those endpoints; the bar split is an editorial score/audio inference.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The forceful paragraph turns inward
transitions.how: After successive expansions, the sextet reduces its weight and exposes more of the individual lines. The ensemble does not change: Schoenberg creates the contrast through dynamics, phrase shape and changing chromatic harmony. The quieter paragraph remains connected to the confession rather than offering a closed, independent movement.
transitions.evidence: The report falls after the 3:05–3:20 crest and has a major boundary at 4:02. The original score and composer’s analysis supply the continuous thematic context; no exact cadence or bar number is attached to this listening boundary.

transitions.title: A crest opens onto E major
transitions.how: The intense passage broadens before the E-major contrast. Longer melodic notes and a quieter, gently moving accompaniment alter the weight of the sextet without changing its instrumentation. In Schoenberg’s account, the new theme belongs to the woman’s longing for fulfilment: its major colour is a local contrast, not the final transformation into D major.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 12–13, Breiter and Etwas ruhiger; composer’s analysis, example 7. The report drops after 6:35–6:40 and changes at 6:52/7:08. The 6:52 marker is approximate.

transitions.title: The gentler episode loses its stability
transitions.how: The long contrasting span does not remain in one settled major colour. Returning fragments and renewed swells break its gentler continuity, while quiet intervals separate the stronger gestures. The connection is made through thematic transformation within the same six-part texture, not a sudden replacement of one instrumental group by another.
transitions.evidence: The report changes at 11:38 and 11:56, followed by the strong 12:25 rise. The composer’s analysis supplies the continuing thematic relationships; this is a broad listening boundary, not a bar-aligned recapitulation.

transitions.title: Agitation contracts to a single bass note
transitions.how: The separated late gestures diminish into an E♭-minor sonority. Upper voices withdraw until B♭ remains in the bass, preparing the startling D-major answer at bar 229. The record ends before that answer, so its physical side break must not be heard as a completed tonal cadence or a separate movement ending.
transitions.evidence: Original score pp. 24–26 and Schoenberg’s analysis, examples 9–11. The report has a boundary at 13:54, followed by very quiet 14:10–14:40 windows. The final B♭ is not assigned an exact timestamp.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos begin; one of each pair carries the descending figure while the other supplies the repeated lower support.
The violins join the lower-string figure; the six parts remain individually written, not doubled string sections.
The expanding first span uses the complete sextet; melodic fragments and supporting lines pass among the players.
The E-major episode sets a longer upper line against gently moving inner strings and a separate bass.
The same six-part ensemble supplies the late alternation of quiet gestures and stronger expansions.
Upper gestures taper over the lower harmony; the last surviving B♭ belongs to the second cello before the LP break.

composer.epithet: A Viennese teacher who took motivic development beyond the key signature, then made twelve notes carry the work of a tonal system.
facts: Largely self-taught; counterpoint lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky; close study of Bach, Beethoven, Brahms and Wagner
Berg and Webern from 1904 · Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33 · University of California, Los Angeles, 1936–44
Developing variation · free atonality · twelve-tone composition · Sprechstimme
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
Arnold Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt, the son of a Jewish shopkeeper, and learned the violin as a child. When his father died in 1889, the family’s finances made extended formal study impossible. He worked in a bank from 1891 to 1895, played chamber music with friends and learned composition by examining scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him counterpoint lessons. Schoenberg’s later teaching grew from this close reading: he explained, with unusual insistence, what each note in Bach, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms was doing.

In the 1890s the apparent opposition between Brahms and Wagner organised Viennese musical argument. Schoenberg took techniques from both. From Brahms came the continuous alteration of a small motif, later described as developing variation; from Wagner came chromatic harmony whose resolution could be postponed across an entire scene. Verklärte Nacht, written in 1899 for string sextet, applies these procedures to Richard Dehmel’s poem about a woman confessing to her lover that she carries another man’s child. The opening D minor eventually transforms into D major, supplying the work’s large-scale harmonic argument.
